 "identityCheck":"The title printed in the text, Practitioner Usage, Applications, and Understanding of Wearable GPS and Accelerometer Technology in Team Sports (Dawson L et al.), matches the filename and crossrefTitle.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"This cross-sectional online survey (May 2021 to May 2022) asked 72 practitioners who regularly use GPS and accelerometer load monitoring in outdoor or invasion team sports about their usage, understanding and opinions. All respondents supported GPS use, 87.5% agreed that wearable data informs training prescription, and only 50% agreed that it influences decisions in competition. GPS metrics were used and understood more than accelerometer-derived metrics, with 47.2% agreeing that accelerometer metrics are easy to understand, and 93.1% said wearable technology needs further standardization.",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a self-selected survey of practitioners' opinions and reported practice, not a measure of athlete load, validity or outcomes. Respondents were not asked to separate sports or competition levels, and self-rated understanding did not match the quality of the definitions they gave.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read these practitioner opinions as evidence about how accurate or useful the wearable metrics are, when the survey measured what practitioners believe and do, not whether the metrics are valid.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Dawson L, McErlain-Naylor SA, Devereux G, Beato M. Practitioner Usage, Applications, and Understanding of Wearable GPS and Accelerometer Technology in Team Sports. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004781",
   "abstract":"The survey investigated how 72 practitioners in team sports use, apply and understand trunk-mounted GPS and accelerometer technology for athlete load monitoring. Practitioners widely supported GPS, and most used wearable data to inform training, but fewer used it for competition decisions. Accelerometer-derived metrics were used less and understood less well than GPS metrics, and practitioners asked for more standardization and education.",
   "tldr":"Most team sport practitioners in this survey use wearable data to plan training, but far fewer use it for match decisions. Accelerometer-derived metrics are less well understood than GPS metrics, so staff should check what each metric measures before acting on it.",
   "methods":"A cross-sectional online survey, distributed through social networking, sport science and coaching networks, and online noticeboards from May 2021 to May 2022, asked 72 practitioners with regular GPS and accelerometer load monitoring experience about usage, applications and understanding, using Likert, rating and open questions. Open responses were analysed with six-phase thematic analysis, and two researchers independently categorised the quality of respondents' metric definitions.",
   "findings":"All 72 respondents supported GPS use in their sport, and 70.8% agreed it is important for success. 87.5% agreed that wearable data informs training prescription, but only 50% agreed it influences decisions in competition. Total distance was the most common metric (93% of respondents), and 84.7% found GPS metrics easy to understand compared with 47.2% for accelerometer-derived metrics. Practitioners' self-rated understanding did not track the quality of their definitions.",
   "limitations":"The sample is self-selected, so response bias is likely, and the authors note that respondents may have strong opinions on the topic. Because respondents could select several sports and competition levels, results could not be compared by sport or level, and role-specific views were not separated. Questions were not compulsory and the completion rate cannot be calculated.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff should learn what accelerometer-derived metrics measure before using them to prescribe training, since many practitioners rated their understanding highly but gave inaccurate definitions. Consistent data collection (same unit, same player, same garment) and shared definitions across staff are needed before wearable data are compared between sessions.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Before a practitioner uses an accelerometer-derived load metric to plan sessions, they should confirm how the metric is calculated and check it against GPS measures such as total distance and high-speed running. Each player should use the same unit and garment, because the authors note that brands use different formulas and interunit variation can mislead comparisons.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return to sport. It surveys practitioners about training load monitoring and reports no injured players, rehabilitation outcomes or return-to-play decisions. Respondents said accelerometer data informed injury rehabilitation (median 6 of 10), but the survey does not test whether these data guide return to play."
 }
}

26	metrics for athlete load monitoring. Such information can be used to improve the implementation of this technology in team sport

Abstract
Dawson, L, McErlain-Naylor, SA, Devereux, G, and Beato, M. Practitioner usage, applications, and understanding of wearable GPS
and accelerometer technology in team sports. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000–000, 2024—Monitoring training load is essential for
optimizing the performance of athletes, allowing practitioners to assess training programs, monitor athlete progress, and minimize
2eTwL/ZFZCxD413lizA9vtUIjMVkNF8F/e29KG4jsPwh382C35tqtwKdeh21n/tkVAV08GvvOJ+sJCFOPfdY+hlYkKNuETHd/BLe
the risk of injury and overtraining. However, there is no universal method for training load monitoring, and the adoption of wearable
global positioning system (GPS) and accelerometer technology in team sports has increased the volume of data and, therefore, the
number of possible approaches. This survey investigated the usage, applications, and understanding of this technology by team
sports practitioners. Seventy-two practitioners involved in team and athlete performance monitoring using GPS and accelerometer
technology completed the survey. All respondents reported supporting the use of GPS technology in their sport, with 70.8% feeling
that GPS technology is important for success. Results showed that 87.5% of respondents use data from wearable technology to
inform training prescription, although only 50% use the data to influence decisions in competition. In addition, results showed that
GPS metrics are used more than accelerometer-derived metrics; however, both are used regularly. Discrepancies in accelerometer
usage highlighted concerns about practitioners’ understanding of accelerometer-derived metrics. This survey gained insight into
usage, application, understanding, practitioner needs, and concerns and criticisms surrounding the use of GPS and accelerometer
metrics for athlete load monitoring. Such information can be used to improve the implementation of this technology in team sport
monitoring and highlight gaps in the literature that will help to design future studies to support practitioner needs.

 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"This retrospective analysis used publicly available NFL Combine data from 1999 to 2020 and split the players into a training set (n = 2,071) and a test set (n = 2,070). Regression equations predicted 9.14-m, 9.14 to 18.29-m, 18.29 to 36.58-m and 36.58-m sprint times from vertical jump, broad jump, height and body mass, with adjusted R2 values of 0.74 to 0.84. In the test set, biases were -0.05 to -0.02 s and RMSE was 0.05 to 0.12 s, with 5 to 6% of predictions outside the limits of agreement.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The equations come from one retrospective data set of NFL Combine testing, using a hand-trigger, three-point sprint start and a Vertec vertical jump, and they were fitted with stepwise regression on a single random split. Their accuracy in other squads, other sprint setups or other jump methods is untested, and the paper's own sample counts disagree (see limitations).",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the predicted sprint time as the athlete's true sprint ability, or read a faster or slower actual time as a technical or physical deficit, when 5 to 6% of predictions fell outside the agreement limits and the authors say the gap needs further investigation.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Agar-Newman DJ, MacRae F, Tsai M-C, Klimstra M. Predicting Sprint Performance From the Vertical and Horizontal Jumps in National Football League Combine Athletes. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(8):1433-1439.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004799",
   "abstract":"The authors built regression equations that predict sprint times over four segments of the NFL Combine 36.58-m sprint from vertical jump, broad jump, height and body mass. Models were developed on half of the data and tested on the other half. The equations explained 74 to 84% of the variance in segment times, with small biases and 5 to 6% of predictions outside the limits of agreement.",
   "tldr":"Sprint times over the 36.58-m (40-yard) sprint and its splits can be estimated from jump tests and body size, which helps when a player did not sprint. The estimates are useful for spotting a difference between predicted and actual speed, but not for exact individual times.",
   "methods":"Retrospective NFL Combine data (1999 to 2020) from a public website were filtered to players with complete records. Backward stepwise multiple regression on a training set predicted the four sprint segments from vertical jump, broad jump, height and body mass, and Bland-Altman analysis compared predicted and measured times on a test set.",
   "findings":"Adjusted R2 was 0.76 for 9.14-m time, 0.74 for 9.14 to 18.29-m time, 0.79 for 18.29 to 36.58-m time and 0.84 for 36.58-m time, with standard errors of 0.05 to 0.12 s. Biases in the test set were -0.05, -0.04, -0.02 and -0.02 s, with RMSE of 0.07, 0.05, 0.07 and 0.12 s. Mass and broad jump had the largest standardized coefficients, and 5.0 to 5.8% of predictions in each segment lay outside the limits of agreement.",
   "limitations":"The abstract and Subjects section give 4,149 players, Table 1 and the training and test split give 4,141, and the Statistical Analyses section gives 4,071 complete sets of data, so the final sample size is not consistent. The data come from a single source, the NFL Combine uses a hand-trigger start, and the Vertec jump height may be inflated compared with force plate methods, as the authors note. The equations were fitted with stepwise regression on one split, and the authors caution against extrapolating beyond the performance levels studied. The PDF prints the year 2024, which matches the Crossref record.",
   "practicalImplications":"The equations let staff estimate sprint times when a 36.58-m sprint was not run and compare an athlete's measured time with the predicted time. A player who runs faster or slower than predicted can prompt a look at technique or physical limits, but the 5 to 6% of predictions outside the agreement limits show that the estimates need checking against measured sprints.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Staff preparing players for the Combine can use vertical jump, broad jump and body mass to estimate each sprint segment and see where a player's sprint may be below or above what his jumps predict. A gap between predicted and measured sprint times is a reason to look at technique or force application, not a fixed training target.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return to sport. It uses draft-eligible players tested at the Combine and reports no injured athletes, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes, so the prediction equations should not be used to judge readiness after injury."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q38",
 "sourceFile":"Progressive Workload Periodization Maximizes Effects of Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Muscle Injury Risk Factors.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title printed in the text, Progressive Workload Periodization Maximizes Effects of Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Muscle Injury Risk Factors (Severo-Silveira L et al.), matches the filename and crossrefTitle.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance"],
 "sports":["Rugby"],
 "populations":["Healthy Athletes","Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"In this randomized trial with no control group, 21 premier league rugby union players completed an 8-week Nordic hamstring exercise program either at a constant workload or with progressive workload. Only the progressive group improved concentric and eccentric hamstring peak torque (7 to 8%, small effects) and the conventional and functional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios (6 to 7%, moderate effects). Both groups increased biceps femoris long head thickness (about 7%) and fascicle length (about 7% and 10%), and no between-group difference reached statistical significance.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The trial is small (21 players from one squad), has no control group, and does not measure injury incidence, which the authors could not follow across the season. No between-group difference was statistically significant, so the advantage of progressive workload rests on magnitude-based inference and the outcomes are risk-factor measures rather than injuries.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could take the title's claim that progressive workload maximizes the program as established, when the between-group differences were not statistically significant in 21 players and the injury outcome was not measured.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2018,
   "citation":"Severo-Silveira L, Dornelles MP, Lima-e-Silva FX, Marchiori CL, Medeiros TM, Pappas E, et al. Progressive Workload Periodization Maximizes Effects of Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Muscle Injury Risk Factors. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2018.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000002849",
   "abstract":"The study compared constant and progressive workload 8-week Nordic hamstring exercise programs in 21 rugby union players on hamstring strength and biceps femoris long head architecture. Only the progressive group increased hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios, while both groups increased muscle thickness and fascicle length. The authors conclude that progressive workload was superior for strength and fascicle length, although the between-group differences were not statistically significant.",
   "tldr":"Nordic hamstring training improved hamstring muscle size and length in these rugby players whether the workload was constant or progressive. Only the progressive program also improved hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios, but the between-group differences were not statistically significant.",
   "methods":"Twenty-one rugby union players were randomized to a constant or progressive workload 8-week Nordic hamstring exercise program, with two sessions per week and no control group. Isokinetic knee strength and biceps femoris long head thickness, pennation angle and fascicle length (ultrasound) were measured within one week before and after the program, and within-group changes were compared with magnitude-based inference.",
   "findings":"Only the progressive group increased concentric hamstring peak torque (7.7%, p = 0.004, d = 0.42) and eccentric hamstring peak torque (6.9%, p = 0.041, d = 0.39), along with conventional (7.6%, p = 0.015) and functional (6.6%, p = 0.026) hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios. Both groups increased biceps femoris long head thickness (about 7%) and fascicle length, with the constant group rising from 10.48 to 11.26 cm and the progressive group from 11.13 to 12.26 cm. No between-group difference was statistically significant.",
   "limitations":"The group sizes are reported inconsistently: the text gives 11 constant and 10 progressive players, but Table 1 gives 10 constant and 11 progressive, and the leg counts (20 and 22) match the table. The abstract gives an 8% constant-group fascicle length increase, while Table 1 gives 7.44%. There is no control group, no injury outcome and no significant between-group difference. The PDF prints the year 2018, while the Crossref record lists 2021; the PDF year is used here.",
   "practicalImplications":"Nordic hamstring training improves hamstring fascicle length and thickness in trained rugby players, and a progressive workload may add to the gains in hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quadriceps balance. Because the progressive advantage was not statistically significant, staff should treat progression as a sensible way to plan the program rather than a proven method to prevent injury.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Plan Nordic hamstring training as a progressed block, not a fixed set of repetitions, because the progressive group showed larger strength and fascicle gains. The paper shows the progression scheme only in a figure, so copy the exact sets and repetitions from the source rather than from this record.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested risk factors in players without current injuries and reports no rehabilitation, reinjury or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot show when an injured hamstring is ready for competition."
 }
}

The abstract gives an 8% constant-group fascicle length increase, while Table 1 gives 7.44%. There is no control group, no injury outcome and no significant between-group difference. The PDF prints the year 2018, while the Crossref record lists 2021; the PDF year is used here.",
   "practicalImplications":"Nordic hamstring training improves hamstring fascicle length and thickness in trained rugby players, and a progressive workload may add to the gains in hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quadriceps balance. Because the progressive advantage was not statistically significant, staff should treat progression as a sensible way to plan the program rather than a proven method to prevent injury.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Plan Nordic hamstring training as a progressed block, not a fixed set of repetitions, because the progressive group showed larger strength and fascicle gains. The paper shows the progression scheme only in a figure, so copy the exact sets and repetitions from the source rather than from this record.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested risk factors in players without current injuries and reports no rehabilitation, reinjury or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot show when an injured hamstring is ready for competition."
 }

 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",

 "evidenceSummary":"This case report describes one 23-year-old male professional American football placekicker who had a near-complete proximal rectus femoris tendon tear after a noncontact injury in practice. Ultrasound and MRI showed about 1 cm of retraction of the direct head and a high-grade partial tear of the indirect head, and he chose open surgical repair 2 weeks after injury. At 6 months he had a minor hip flexion strength deficit compared with the other leg and had returned to running and kicking pain-free.",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a single athlete with one follow-up point, and the strength deficit is described only as minor without a measured value. The athlete chose surgery after a second opinion, so the case cannot compare operative with nonoperative care or show what is typical for kickers.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the good 6-month outcome as proof that surgery is the right route for a placekicker, when this is one case, the surgery followed a second opinion, and no nonoperative comparison was made.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Noble-Taylor K, Price M, McInnis K. Proximal Rectus Femoris Tendon Tear in a Professional Football Placekicker: A Case Report. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2023;22(6):187-190.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000001071",
   "abstract":"The authors describe a proximal rectus femoris tendon tear in a professional American football placekicker, with imaging, surgical repair and return to kicking. The tear involved both the direct and indirect heads, which is rarely reported in this sport. The athlete returned to running and pain-free kicking at about 6 months.",
   "tldr":"A professional placekicker with a near-complete proximal rectus femoris tear returned to pain-free kicking about 6 months after surgical repair. This single case shows one successful surgical route, but it does not settle the choice between surgery and nonoperative care.",
   "methods":"A case report of one professional placekicker, with clinical examination, point-of-care ultrasound and MRI at presentation. The athlete then underwent open surgical repair 2 weeks after injury at an outside clinic, followed by a graduated rehabilitation program with follow-up at 6 months.",
   "findings":"Ultrasound showed near-complete disruption of the direct head with about 1 cm of retraction, and MRI showed a high-grade near full-thickness partial tear of the direct and indirect attachments. The athlete was non-weight-bearing for 6 weeks after surgery, began eccentric strengthening at 8 weeks, returned to kicking at 3 months and had a minor hip flexion deficit at 6 months.",
   "limitations":"Only one athlete is described, and the follow-up is a single point at 6 months with no measured strength values. The authors cite two NFL punter cases, an 11-athlete NFL case series with no pure placekickers, and professional soccer surgical reports, so the evidence base for placekickers is thin. The PDF prints the year 2023, which matches the Crossref record.",
   "practicalImplications":"For a kicker with a near-complete proximal rectus femoris tear, this case shows a surgical route with progressive hip motion, isometric then eccentric loading, and a return to kicking at about 3 months. The authors stress that the choice between surgery and nonoperative care depends on injury timing, career stage and goals, so staff should use this as one example of the process rather than a timeline to follow.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: This case gives one kicker's sequence after surgical repair: non-weight-bearing for 6 weeks, eccentric strengthening from about week 8 and kicking from month 3. It is useful for planning kicking work after a similar injury, but it is one athlete's timeline, not a standard for placekickers.",
   "rtp":"The study can inform return to sport in one professional placekicker: the authors use pain-controlled hip motion and strength close to the other side as the criterion, and this athlete was kicking pain-free at 6 months. It cannot set a return-to-play timeline for other kickers or for nonoperative management, because it describes one surgical case."
 }
}

Diagnosis of RF tendon injuries is typically made clinically
based on mechanism of injury and physical examination.
MRI is the criterion standard imaging modality for confirming
the diagnosis and defining tendon injury characteristics, as in
the presented case (13). Musculoskeletal ultrasonography
(US) is a useful diagnostic point-of-care tool, especially when
there is edema or hematoma, and can assist in monitoring the
recovery of RF injuries (14). However, imaging of the RF indi-
rect head, given its oblique path to the acetabulum, is challeng-
ing, even for experienced musculoskeletal sonographers. Plain
radiographs may be useful to rule out associated bone avulsion
injuries, especially in the skeletally immature athlete.
Characteristic MRI grading of myotendinous injury ranges
from I to III (13,15). Grade I tears are defined by high-intensity
signal at an intact myotendinous junction. Grade II tears are de-
fined by partial disruption of the myotendinous junction. Grade
III tears involve complete myotendinous disruption with or with-
out retraction (11,13). A newer grading system proposed by
British Athletics describes a more detailed classification based
on extent (grades 0 to 4) and site of injury (a, myofascial; b,
muscular/musculotendinous; c, intratendinous) (15,16). Based
on this system, this case illustrates a grade 3c, near complete
intratendinous tear with retraction.
Proximal RF tendon tears are typically managed nonoperatively.
This includes an initial rest period (usually 3 to 5 d) that may involve
crutches if ambulation is painful. Pain is managed with ice,
modalities, and analgesic medications. This is followed by a
comprehensive rehabilitation protocol involving therapeutic
exercise, including core stability, isometric progressing to ec-
centric and concentric strengthening of the hip flexors and
knee extensors, and stretching of the iliopsoas and quadriceps
musculature (11). Graduated return to sport- and position-specific
exercise is performed. Return to sport is appropriate when the
athlete's pain is controlled with near normal hip range of mo-
tion and strength compared with the contralateral side.

 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title printed in the text, Public Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Knowledge: Sources, Accuracy and Confidence (Zurlinden T et al.), matches the filename and crossrefTitle.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains":["Brain Health & Psychology","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"This cross-sectional online survey included 529 adults from the general public in the United States, recruited through university research credit, Amazon MTurk and social media. Average CTE knowledge accuracy was 48.02% (SD 0.23), with the lowest accuracy on the cause and diagnosis of CTE. Confidence in CTE knowledge was positively correlated with comfort allowing a child to play a high-contact sport (r = 0.199, p <= 0.001), while accuracy was not correlated with that comfort (r = 0.004), and television/movies and professional athletes were associated with higher accuracy.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The sample is the general public, not athletes, and the outcomes are self-reported knowledge, confidence and comfort rather than athlete health. Answers were true/false with a free-text 'other' option, and the recruitment and the online format limit how far the results generalize.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the low accuracy as evidence about how athletes or families actually behave around sport, when the survey measured public knowledge and stated comfort, not athlete health or participation decisions.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Zurlinden T, Falletta G, Schneider K, Sorrell AE, Savransky A, Everhart DE. Public Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Knowledge: Sources, Accuracy and Confidence. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2024;23(1):23-28.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000001131",
   "abstract":"The survey measured public knowledge of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the sources people use, their confidence in that knowledge, and their comfort allowing a child to play a high-contact sport. Average accuracy was 48%, and the most common errors concerned the cause and diagnosis of CTE. Confidence was linked with comfort about children playing high-contact sport, but accuracy was not.",
   "tldr":"Members of the public in this survey were often wrong about CTE, especially its cause and how it is diagnosed, yet those who were more confident in their knowledge were more comfortable letting children play high-contact sport. Television, movies and professional athletes were the sources linked with more accurate knowledge, while social media was linked with less accurate knowledge.",
   "methods":"An online survey of 530 participants was analysed, with 529 reported in the abstract and in Table 1. Participants answered six true/false CTE knowledge items (two taken from Merz et al. and four written from the Sports Neuropsychology Society fact sheet), rated their confidence and comfort on 0 to 100 scales, and estimated the share of their CTE information from each source. Total accuracy and item-level accuracy were calculated, and correlations were used to relate sources, confidence, accuracy and comfort.",
   "findings":"Average CTE knowledge accuracy was 48.02%. Only 33.01% correctly rated that CTE cannot be caused by a single injury, 33.97% that it cannot develop without a head injury, and 33.21% that it can be diagnosed only after death, while 70.69% correctly said it cannot be treated. Confidence was positively correlated with comfort allowing a child to play high-contact sport (r = 0.199, p <= 0.001), but accuracy was not (r = 0.004). Television/movies (r = 0.088) and professional athletes (r = 0.127) were linked with higher accuracy, and social media with lower accuracy (r = -0.181).",
   "limitations":"Participants were self-selected online volunteers and the authors could not control for health literacy, English literacy or computer access. The true/false format and the 'other' category limit what can be learned about sources, and self-report may not match behaviour. The text gives 529 participants in the abstract and Table 1 but 530 in the Methods. The Discussion says 68.90% believed sport alone could cause CTE, while Table 2 implies about 66% gave the wrong answer on that item (33.97% correct). The PDF prints the year 2024, which matches the Crossref record.",
   "practicalImplications":"Clinicians and sport staff should correct common CTE misconceptions when they talk with athletes and families, especially that CTE comes from a single injury or from sport alone, and that it can be diagnosed in life. Because confidence was not linked with accuracy, staff should not assume that a parent's certainty about CTE reflects correct knowledge.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: This study does not measure training or performance. Its practical value for performance and medical staff is in education, since the authors suggest that clinicians and staff raise CTE facts with athletes and families when sport participation is discussed.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return to sport. It surveys members of the public about CTE and reports no injured athletes, concussion management or return-to-play outcomes."
 }
}

I checked all eight records and corrected each one. None of the decisions changed. Records are in `verified/Q33.json` to `verified/Q40.json`, and the build script is `helpers/v05/apply.py`.

- **Q33**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The PDF says 2024 but Crossref says 2025, so I kept 2024 and flagged the difference. I also softened the overstated claims in the TLDR and the caution note. The draft left out that running backs did not differ from defensive backs and wide receivers on two speed measures, so I added it.
- **Q34**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The PDF says 2025 but Crossref says 2026, so I kept 2025. The TLDR called the gynoid region the "lower trunk"; it is the hips and upper thighs. The paper contradicts itself on whether defensive linemen lost lean mass, and several table rows look copied in error. Bone mineral content and gynoid fat numbers from this paper should not be quoted.
- **Q35**: DEGRADED confirmed, CORRECTED, high. The PDF is the article the filename names (JSSM 2017;16:407-413), but the external DOI belongs to the same authors' force-time paper, which this PDF lists as a separate reference. The DOI stays empty and the operator needs to look up the real one. I also fixed two errors: there were four sessions in total, including the 1RM session, not four after it. And the hang high pull did not beat the hang power clean at 80% load.
- **Q36**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, normal. I removed advice the paper does not support (checking accelerometer metrics against GPS measures) and added Soccer and Rugby to the sports. The survey gives two different figures for accelerometer metric use (39% and 56%), which I noted.
- **Q37**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, normal. The standard error range is 0.04 to 0.12 s, not 0.05 to 0.12 s. I also noted the paper's conflicting sample counts.
- **Q38**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The PDF says 2018 but Crossref says 2021, so I kept 2018. The methods were wrong in two places:
  - 37 players agreed to take part and only 21 completed. The draft said 21 were randomized.
  - The magnitude-based statistics were used for the comparison between groups, not within groups.

  I also added the dropout and that both legs were counted separately. I softened the claims that the progressive program works better, since no difference between the groups was statistically significant.
- **Q39**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high (return-to-play case). The return-to-sport field said the authors used a clearance rule for this athlete. That rule is actually their general statement about non-surgical care. The paper does not report return to competition or how this athlete was cleared.
- **Q40**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high (CTE). The draft said knowledge answers had a free-text "other" option; that option was only for information sources. I added the finding that confidence was unrelated to accuracy. Overall accuracy of 48% on true/false questions is close to guessing, and 9.26% had never heard of CTE but still had to answer. That reading is my inference, not the authors', and it is flagged as such.
